claim: A typical Escherichia coli cell is propelled by a bundle composed of multiple flagella.
source: A typical Escherichia coli cell is propelled by a bundle composed of multiple flagella.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of bacterial motility, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Each flagellum is controlled by a rotary motor that can switch between clockwise (CW) and counter-clockwise (CCW) rotation.
source: Each flagellum is controlled by a rotary motor that can switch between clockwise (CW) and counter-clockwise (CCW) rotation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial flagellar motors, supported by citation to Berg, 2004.

claim: When flagella on a cell rotate CCW, the cell swims along an approximately straight path called a 'run'.
source: When flagella on a cell rotate CCW, the cell swims along an approximately straight path called a 'run'.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial swimming behavior, supported by citation to Macnab and Ornston, 1977.

claim: When some of the flagella rotate CW, the bundle is disrupted causing an abrupt change in direction called a 'tumble'.
source: When some of the flagella rotate CW, the bundle is disrupted causing an abrupt change in direction called a 'tumble' (Macnab and Ornston, 1977).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial swimming behavior, supported by citation to Macnab and Ornston, 1977.

claim: E. coli modulates the probability of being in one of these two swimming states in response to its environment, allowing it to navigate chemical, temperature, and light gradients.
source: E. coli modulates the probability of being in one of these two swimming states in response to its environment, allowing it to navigate chemical, temperature, and light gradients (Berg and Brown, 1972; Berg, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial chemotaxis, supported by citations to Berg and Brown, 1972 and Berg, 2004.

claim: At any point in time, the probability that a flagellar motor rotates CW is determined by the concentration of phosphorylated signaling protein CheY (CheY-P).
source: At any point in time, the probability that a flagellar motor rotates CW is determined by the concentration of phosphorylated signaling protein CheY (CheY-P).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemotaxis signaling pathway.

claim: The number of flagella on an individual swimming cell can vary greatly, from one to more than ten.
source: The number of flagella on an individual swimming cell can vary greatly, from one to more than ten (Cohen-Ben-Lulu et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cohen-Ben-Lulu et al., 2008 and by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The only direct measurements of flagellar dynamics in swimming cells have been limited to short durations (∼1 s).
source: The only direct measurements of flagellar dynamics in swimming cells have been limited to short durations (∼1 s) (Turner et al., 2000; Darnton et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2000 and Darnton et al., 2007.

claim: Most theoretical models of bacterial chemotaxis are limited to treating an individual motor, or simply assume that all cells have a single flagellum.
source: As a result, most theoretical models of bacterial chemotaxis are limited to treating an individual motor, or simply assume that all cells have a single flagellum (Bray et al., 2007; Kalinin et al., 2009; Matthaus et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Flores et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical modeling papers.

claim: One theoretical model invokes a 'voting' mechanism, in which cells tumble only if a majority of flagella rotate CW.
source: One such model invokes a 'voting' mechanism, in which cells tumble only if a majority of flagella rotate CW (Ishihara et al., 1983; Spiro et al., 1997; Andrews et al., 2006; Vladimirov et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical papers proposing the voting mechanism.

claim: Turner et al. established that CW rotation of a single flagellum is sufficient to 'veto' a run.
source: However, by observing fluorescently labeled flagella during individual tumbles, Turner et al. established that CW rotation of a single flagellum is sufficient to 'veto' a run (Turner et al., 2000) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2000 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Wild-type cells with multiple flagella deviate significantly from the veto model.
source: Wild-type cells (solid black circles) with multiple flagella deviate significantly from the model (p=0.0003, N = 69 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p=0.0003) from 69 cells, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CheY* cells match the veto model.
source: CheY* cells (open gray circles; N = 46 cells) match the model (p=0.77).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p=0.77) from 46 cells, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: More than half of tumbles in multi-flagellated cells (56%, 117/210 events) involved multiple CW flagella.
source: However, we also observed that more than half of tumbles in multi-flagellated cells (56%, 117/210 events) actually involved multiple CW flagella.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct experimental observation and quantification of 210 tumble events.

claim: The number of CW flagella 'participating' in a tumble was significantly larger than would be expected if flagella were independently switching.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, the number of CW flagella 'participating' in a tumble (black circles) was significantly larger than would be expected if flagella were independently switching (gray dashed line, obtained from simulations of a cell with independent flagella; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data to simulations, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the rotational directions of pairs of flagella on the same cell.
source: We found a significant correlation between the rotational directions of pairs of flagella on the same cell (Figure 2D, black data points).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The correlation between flagella persisted for ∼1 s, the average duration of a tumble.
source: This correlation persisted for ∼1 s, the average duration of a tumble.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the correlation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Terasawa et al. observed correlations between individual motors on the same cell by monitoring beads attached to flagellar stubs on surface-immobilized cells.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous observations by Terasawa et al. on surface-immobilized cells (Terasawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Terasawa et al., 2011.

claim: Cells with a single curly-1 flagellum still tumbled 82% of the time.
source: However, in our measurements we observed that cells with a single CW flagellum in the curly-1 state still tumbled 82% of the time (44 s of cumulative time in which one flagellum was in the curly-1 state; Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 44 seconds of cumulative observation time, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Terasawa et al. observed that mutant cells, in which the concentration of CheY-P was decoupled from the chemotaxis network, displayed no correlations.
source: Terasawa et al. observed that mutant cells, in which the concentration of CheY-P was decoupled from the chemotaxis network, displayed no correlations (Terasawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Terasawa et al., 2011.

claim: Flagellar switching appears far less correlated in CheY* cells than in wild-type cells.
source: Upon inspection, flagellar switching appears far less correlated than in wild-type cells (Figure 2D, compare black and gray data points).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data between wild-type and CheY* cells shown in Figure 2D.

claim: On average, fewer CW rotating flagella participated in tumbles in the CheY* strain compared to wild-type.
source: Comparing 54 wild-type and 24 CheY* cells with the same mean CW biases (0.11 ± 0.07 vs 0.11 ± 0.07, mean ± SD) we found that, on average, fewer CW rotating flagella participated in tumbles in the CheY* strain (Figure 2C, open circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing 54 wild-type and 24 CheY* cells, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of participating flagella in the CheY* strain closely matched the expectation for cells with independently switching flagella.
source: Moreover, the number of participating flagella in the CheY* strain closely matched the expectation for cells with independently switching flagella (Figure 2C, dashed line).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data to simulations, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When the signal for flagellar motors to switch their rotational state is decoupled from the chemotaxis network, the motors switch independently.
source: Our results indicate that when the signal for flagellar motors to switch their rotational state is decoupled from the chemotaxis network, the motors switch independently.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results comparing wild-type and CheY* cells.

claim: CheY* cells adhere to the simple veto model.
source: As shown in the plot of η in Figure 1D (open circles), CheY* cells indeed match the veto model closely (η = −0.08 ± 0.15, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, with quantitative measure η = −0.08 ± 0.15.

claim: The existence of correlations between flagella states in wild-type cells may explain why cells with multiple flagella deviate from the veto model.
source: The existence of correlations between flagella states in wild-type cells may thus explain why cells with multiple flagella deviate from the veto model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of wild-type and CheY* cell behavior.

claim: The effective number of flagella Neff is consistently smaller than the actual flagellar number Nflag in wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with this picture, the effective number of flagella Neff is consistently smaller than the actual flagellar number Nflag (Figure 3C, black circles; Neff can be approximated by Neff = 1.27 × Nflag0.5, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and the empirical fit shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Estimating Neff for CheY* cells produces values very close to the original flagellar number Nflag.
source: As a control, estimating Neff for CheY* cells produces values very close to the original flagellar number Nflag (Figure 3B, solid line and Figure 3C, open circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: In wild-type cells, CheY-P levels are subject to phosphorylation and de-phosphorylation reactions by chemotaxis network components and are believed to fluctuate in time.
source: In wild-type cells, CheY-P levels are subject to phosphorylation and de-phosphorylation reactions by chemotaxis network components and are believed to fluctuate in time (Korobkova et al., 2006; Sneddon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Korobkova et al., 2006 and Sneddon et al., 2012.

claim: In the CheY* mutant strain, CheY* levels are decoupled from the network and are expected to be constant over the timescales of interest.
source: In contrast, in the mutant strain, CheY* levels are decoupled from the network and are thus expected to be constant over the timescales of interest (Korobkova et al., 2006; Min et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Korobkova et al., 2006 and Min et al., 2009.

claim: Terasawa et al. proposed that fluctuations in CheY-P levels may provide a mechanism by which the CW biases of multiple flagella on a cell can be coupled.
source: Terasawa et al. proposed that fluctuations in CheY-P levels may thus provide a mechanism by which the CW biases of multiple flagella on a cell can be coupled (Terasawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Terasawa et al., 2011.

claim: Stochastic simulations with CheY-P fluctuations reproduced the observed wild-type behavior.
source: We found that, consistently, simulations with CheY-P fluctuations were able to duplicate the observed wild-type behavior, while simulations without fluctuations matched CheY* data and the predictions of the 'naïve' veto model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of stochastic simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Simulations without CheY-P fluctuations matched CheY* data and the predictions of the 'naïve' veto model.
source: We found that, consistently, simulations with CheY-P fluctuations were able to duplicate the observed wild-type behavior, while simulations without fluctuations matched CheY* data and the predictions of the 'naïve' veto model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of stochastic simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Using only two parameters—the amplitude and the characteristic timescale for CheY-P fluctuations—simulations simultaneously reproduced the relation between flagellar number and flagellar participation in tumbles, temporal correlations between flagella, the effective number of flagella in multi-flagellated wild-type cells, and the degree of deviation from the veto model.
source: Specifically, using only two parameters—the amplitude and the characteristic timescale for CheY-P fluctuations (Table 3)—as fitting parameters, our simulations simultaneously reproduced (i) the relation between flagellar number and flagellar participation in tumbles (Figure 2C); (ii) temporal correlations between flagella (Figure 2D); (iii) the effective number of flagella in multi-flagellated wild-type cells (Figure 3C); and (iv) the degree of deviation from the veto model (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of stochastic simulations shown in Figures 2C, 2D, 3C, and 4C.

claim: There is no direct experimental evidence to-date for the CheY-P fluctuations depicted in Figure 4A.
source: Despite the success of this model in reproducing our data, we must acknowledge that there is no direct experimental evidence to-date for the CheY-P fluctuations depicted in Figure 4A.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a limitation in the current evidence.

claim: Fluctuations in CheY-P have been inferred from experimental observations of CW bias in tethered-bead assays.
source: Fluctuations in CheY-P have been inferred from experimental observations of CW bias in tethered-bead assays (Korobkova et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Korobkova et al., 2004.

claim: The fluctuations described by Korobkova et al. are different in their time scale and amplitude from what was found required to produce the observed correlations in flagellar rotational direction.
source: However, the fluctuations described in that study are different in their time scale and amplitude from what we found required to produce the observed correlations in flagellar rotational direction ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and previous work by Korobkova et al.

claim: Hu and Tu proposed that hydrodynamic interactions between nearby flagella could generate correlations in their rotational direction.
source: As an alternative mechanism for the inter-flagellar correlations observed by Terasawa et al. (2011) (and in the present work), Hu and Tu (2013) proposed that hydrodynamic interactions between nearby flagella could also generate correlations in their rotational direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hu and Tu, 2013.

claim: One consequence of the Hu and Tu model is that the flagellar switching rates in a cell with a single flagellum will be different than those in multi-flagellated cells.
source: One consequence of their model is that the flagellar switching rates in a cell with a single flagellum will be different than those in multi-flagellated cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the predictions of the Hu and Tu model.

claim: The number of flagella per cell did not have a significant effect on the switching rates between CCW and CW states.
source: In our experiments, the number of flagella per cell did not have a significant effect on the switching rates between CCW and CW states, nor on the switching rates between different flagellar waveforms (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The number of flagella per cell did not have a significant effect on the switching rates between different flagellar waveforms.
source: In our experiments, the number of flagella per cell did not have a significant effect on the switching rates between CCW and CW states, nor on the switching rates between different flagellar waveforms (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: A mechanism in which chemotaxis network fluctuations engender inter-flagella correlations is more plausible than hydrodynamic interactions.
source: In light of these constraints, we believe a mechanism in which chemotaxis network fluctuations engender inter-flagella correlations to be more plausible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of experimental data with predictions of different models.

claim: Turner et al. observed that, on average, the angular change in swimming direction upon tumbling increases as a function of the number of flagella that leave the bundle.
source: Turner et al. observed that, on average, the angular change in swimming direction upon tumbling increases as a function of the number of flagella that leave the bundle (Turner et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2000.

claim: Vladimirov et al. showed that when the effect of multiple flagella leaving the bundle is incorporated into a theoretical model of bacterial chemotaxis, the chemotactic drift is nearly doubled.
source: Vladimirov et al. showed that when this effect is incorporated into a theoretical model of bacterial chemotaxis, the chemotactic drift is nearly doubled (Vladimirov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vladimirov et al., 2010.

claim: Multi-flagellated wild-type cells tumble significantly less than expected.
source: Our observations that multi-flagellated wild-type cells tumble significantly less than expected also implies that the cell's swimming behavior (and presumably its chemotactic response) is robust against variations in the number of flagella (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The cell's swimming behavior is robust against variations in the number of flagella.
source: Our observations that multi-flagellated wild-type cells tumble significantly less than expected also implies that the cell's swimming behavior (and presumably its chemotactic response) is robust against variations in the number of flagella (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: If cells with many flagella did not behave like cells with fewer flagella, then they would spend the majority of their time tumbling, a behavior that would inhibit chemotaxis.
source: If cells with many flagella did not behave like cells with fewer flagella, then they would spend the majority of their time tumbling, a behavior that would inhibit chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of different swimming behaviors.

claim: E. coli appears to have developed a mechanism to achieve similar tumble biases with a wide range of flagellar number.
source: E. coli thus appears to have developed a mechanism to achieve similar tumble biases with a wide range of flagellar number.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations about the robustness of swimming behavior.

claim: The majority of CCW-to-CW switches caused flagella to transition to the semi-coiled waveform (77%, 164/213 of all flagellar switching events).
source: The majority of CCW-to-CW switches caused flagella to transition to the semi-coiled waveform (77%, 164/213 of all flagellar switching events).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 213 flagellar switching events, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Of flagella that transitioned to semi-coiled, most remained semi-coiled until the motor returned to CCW (71%, 117/164).
source: Of those flagella, most remained semi-coiled until the motor returned to CCW (71%, 117/164), while some instead transitioned to the curly-1 waveform (29%, 47/164).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some fraction of flagella (22%, 47/213) skipped the semi-coiled waveform altogether and transitioned immediately from CCW to curly-1.
source: Some fraction of flagella (22%, 47/213) also skipped the semi-coiled waveform altogether and transitioned immediately from CCW to curly-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The sequence of states from normal to semi-coiled to curly-1 was described by Darnton et al. as a 'canonical tumble'.
source: In particular, the sequence of states from normal to semi-coiled to curly-1 that we observed was described by Darnton et al. (2007) as a 'canonical tumble'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Darnton et al., 2007.

claim: The results are in qualitative agreement with previous observations by Darnton et al.
source: Although we cannot rule out that runs and tumbles in the optical trap are different in some ways than those in free swimming cells (Min et al., 2009), our results are in qualitative agreement with these previous observations.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's results with previous work by Darnton et al.

claim: In a multi-flagellated wild-type cell, a single CW flagellum (either semi-coiled or curly-1) is sufficient to induce a tumble.
source: In a multi-flagellated wild-type cell, a single CW flagellum (either semi-coiled or curly-1) is sufficient to induce a tumble, in agreement with the simple veto model (Turner et al., 2000; Darnton et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to Turner et al., 2000 and Darnton et al., 2007.

claim: The high fraction of CW flagella during tumbles in wild-type cells is in qualitative agreement with previous measurements by Turner et al.
source: The high fraction of CW flagella during tumbles in wild-type cells is in qualitative agreement with previous measurements by Turner et al. (2000), who observed that a majority of tumbles involved multiple flagella leaving the bundle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2000.

claim: The relationship between the chemotaxis signaling network and the CCW/CW rotational bias of the individual flagellar motor is now well mapped.
source: The relationship between the chemotaxis signaling network and the CCW/CW rotational bias of the individual flagellar motor is now well mapped ([Block et al., 1982; Cluzel et al., 2000; Sourjik and Berg, 2002; Yuan et al., 2012]; for a review see Berg, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to key papers in the field.

claim: The chemotaxis signaling network has been described using detailed mathematical models.
source: and has also been described using detailed mathematical models (Emonet et al., 2005; Jiang et al., 2010; Shimizu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling papers.

claim: How the CCW/CW states of individual motors collectively determine the run/tumble swimming behavior of the whole, multi-flagellated cell remains poorly understood.
source: Despite this wealth of knowledge, how the CCW/CW states of individual motors collectively determine the run/tumble swimming behavior of the whole, multi-flagellated cell remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The current study provides the first experimentally-derived mathematical relation between flagellar and whole-cell-swimming states.
source: To the best of our knowledge, the current study provides the first experimentally-derived mathematical relation between flagellar and whole-cell-swimming states.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's contribution.

claim: The distributions of flagella per cell from trapped cells and TEM have very similar means.
source: The distributions from trapped cells (blue, N = 86 cells) and TEM (red, N = 56 cells) have very similar means.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data from two different methods shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When all flagella were in the normal waveform, cells ran 91% of the time.
source: When all flagella were in the normal waveform, cells ran 91% of the time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: When the waveform of a single flagellum was curly-1, and the rest were normal, cells ran 18% of the time.
source: When the waveform of a single flagellum was curly-1, and the rest were normal, cells ran 18% of the time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The veto model corresponds to an AND gate, by which cell runs only occur when all flagella rotate CCW.
source: The veto model corresponds to an AND gate, by which cell runs only occur when all flagella rotate CCW (where CCW = 1, CW = 0, run = 1, and tumble = 0).
evidence: This is a description of the veto model illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A simple mathematical expression relates the cell's run/tumble bias to the number and average rotational state of its flagella.
source: We find that a simple mathematical expression relates the cell's run/tumble bias to the number and average rotational state of its flagella.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Due to inter-flagellar correlations, an 'effective number' of flagella—smaller than the actual number—enters into the relation between run/tumble bias and flagellar state.
source: However, due to inter-flagellar correlations, an 'effective number' of flagella—smaller than the actual number—enters into this relation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Data from a chemotaxis mutant and stochastic modeling suggest that fluctuations of the regulator CheY-P are the source of flagellar correlations.
source: Data from a chemotaxis mutant and stochastic modeling suggest that fluctuations of the regulator CheY-P are the source of flagellar correlations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study, supported by data from CheY* mutant and simulations.

claim: A consequence of inter-flagellar correlations is that run/tumble behavior is only weakly dependent on number of flagella.
source: A consequence of inter-flagellar correlations is that run/tumble behavior is only weakly dependent on number of flagella.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.
